subtopic: STATEMENT ON STRENGTH AND RECRUITING OF ARMED FORCES

speakeroldname: Hon. BROOKE CLAXTON (Minister of National Defence):
subtopic: STATEMENT ON STRENGTH AND RECRUITING OF ARMED FORCES
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, in view of its importance in the national interest I feel that hon. members will wish me to make a statement on the strength and recruiting for the active (or permanent) and reserve forces.
The authorized strength of the three services of the active forces is 42,145 officers and men. At the end of February the strength was 34,276, which is more than three times as large as at the outbreak of war in 1939. This number represents 80 per cent of the strength at present authorized. It is interesting to note that the proportion of regulars on strength compared with the target for March 31, 1949, is the same in Canada as in the United Kingdom. Unlike other countries which still have men who were enlisted for the duration of hostilities or who were called up for a limited period, all Canadian forces are permanent or regular.
It may be pointed out that in Canada as in other countries there has been a tendency since the war to use civilians for work which was previously performed by service personnel but which is obviously of a civilian character. This includes cooks, mess orderlies, clerks, certain mechanics, firefighters and other occupations of a civilian character at permanent establishments. Other civilians are engaged at prevailing rates in the dockyards at Esquimalt and Halifax in constructing married quarters and in general maintenance work.
The present strength of the army reserve forces is 33,369, with 1,829 C.O.T.C., making a total of 35,198. In the naval reserve there are 2.112, with 1,033 in the university naval training division, making 3,145. The air force auxiliary with 722 men is beginning to set up squadrons as ground crews and planes become available.
The total figures for the navy and army reserves and air force auxiliary are about the same as they were up to the period immediately before the war. But now there are also more than a million men and women in Canada who have had military service in the second world war, including a higher proportion of trained air crew than m any other country.
255S

National Defence
Last September a campaign to obtain recruits was set under way across Canada and has since been continued. This campaign included distribution of information, radio and newspaper publicity, exhibitions and parades.
The recruiting campaign has shown good results. During the year 1947 there were 31,688 approaches for active service in the three forces, resulting in 9,240 enlistments. The largest cause of rejection was the high educational standard required for the three services.
The standard has been junior matriculation or its equivalent. This was considered desirable because of the highly technical nature of work in the forces, particularly as a major part of the role of the active forces is related to administration and training. The active forces will serve as a nucleus about which to build a very much larger force should the need arise.
The problem of educational standards is serious. It has been estimated that each year about 6,500 physically fit boys reach 17i, who have junior matriculation and who do not go on to senior matriculation or the universities. To fill up our ranks with boys of this standard would take virtually all the boys having these qualifications-even then, we would not have enough. As it has turned out, we have been getting a very fair proportion. But steps are now being taken to reduce or adjust the educational standards so as to broaden the field; at the same time we shall increase facilities for in-service general education so as to achieve by one means or the other the standards that are necessary.
As to the flow of recruits, this year up to the 15th March, we have obtained a total of 1,625 recruits, of which approximately half are for the army alone. The flow into the army is at the rate required to keep the recruit schools full and to complete the authorized establishment by the time planned. The flow into the navy and air force is less than we require.
Parents and young men should realize that joining our navy, army and air force gives an opportunity for (1) service to Canada; (2) a career with good rates of pay and conditions of service; (3) continuing education and developing trade and other skills; and (4) an excellent pension at a relatively early age.
I am convinced that young men will come forward to fill up the ranks of the active forces.
We also want all the men we can get for the reserve navy and army and the auxiliary air force. The reserve forces are a major part of Canada's defence forces. In the event of

an emergency the reserves would again constitute the framework for the organization of larger active forces. Reserve force training is service of real national importance which should appeal to all young Canadians who are physically fit and are willing to offer their services for part-time training.
Attention should also be called to the remarkable opportunities for training as officers offered in the Canadian service colleges at Royal Roads and R.M.C., Kingston. This year there will be a number of vacancies for boys having senior matriculation or its equivalent. Application should be made by the twenty-second of May. Pay received for summer training should cover the whole cost of education for the second and subsequent years. By this means and through the university officers training plans, it is believed that we will have a large force of highly qualified officers with standards never excelled in this or any other country.
There is no necessity of pointing out today that either from the short or the long term point of view, active and reserve forces of the character which I have described are needed so that we can be ready to meet any emergency and maintain the existence of our country and the freedom of our people, so that we shall continue to say what kind of life we want to lead.
I hope that this effort to fill up our ranks will have the support of all parties, of all veterans of the two wars, and of the country as a whole.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
subtopic: FOREIGN EXCHANGE CONTROL-CANADIANS TAKING UP RESIDENCE IN U.S.
speechtext:
Under the Foreign Exchange Control Act and regulations, a resident of Canada desiring to leave Canada permanently and transfer his assets from Canada is required to apply to the foreign exchange control board for change of status from a "resident" to a "non-resident" for foreign exchange control purposes. Information is not available as to persons applying for change of status to take up permanent residence in the United States as distinct from other United States dollar area countries although the large majority of applications are by persons desiring to take up permanent residence in the United States.
No permit from the board was required by a resident leaving Canada with not more than $150 (including not more than $100 in U.S. funds) up until May 1947. and $25 (including not more than $10 in U.S. funds) since that time. The information available does not

include residents who may have left Canada for permanent residence in the United States or elsewhere who took with them not more than these amounts during the periods indicated but did not make application for change of status.
In addition, a family group is normally dealt with under one application for change of status and no record has been kept of the number of individuals covered by such applications.
Subject to the foregoing, the replies to the questions are as follows:
1.	Number of applications approved for change of status for persons leaving Canada to take up permanent residence in United States dollar area countries-19,315.
2.	The total amount of Canadian dollars and securities declared in the applications referred' to in the answer to question No. 1 and authorized to be transferred from Canada was $46,305,464. Information is not available as to the amount of Canadian dollars and securities which were actually transferred from Canada.
United States dollars are not provided out of Canada's reserves at the official rate of exchange for transfers of capital from Canada by persons leaving Canada to take up permanent residence elsewhere, except for a small amount per applicant to meet travelling and initial expenses. The amount of United States dollars made available by the board for this latter purpose was $6,565,689. The balance was authorized for transfer from Canada only in the form of Canadian domestic securities or in Canadian dollars which the owner, upon becoming a non-resident, could convert into United States dollars in the unofficial market in the United States.
3. No applicant for change of status was permitted to convert $5,000 or more into United States funds in Canada at the official rate of exchange.

In reply to the hon. member for Vancouver East, and also in reply to an inquiry from the senior member for Halifax (Mr. Isnor), I might say that this dispute is a long standing one. speechtext: The leader of my hon. fi iend s party mentioned an amendment to the wheat board act in another place. I said that I would make a statement after the wheat board bill had passed. I am afraid I cannot do so at this time.

Hon. DOUGLAS ABBOTT (Minister of Finance) moved the second reading of Bill No. 172. to amend the Excise Tax Act.
Mr. J. M. MACDONNELL (Muskoka-Ontario). Mr. Speaker, I know there are some people in this house who believe that this bill has been quite adequately discussed in committee, and I do not propose to take very much time. I had that opinion when I came into the chamber; and since the threat of the Prime Minister, though delivered as the Minister of Labour would say "in a kindly way," I feel still more strongly that I should be brief, and I shall be brief. Nevertheless I feel that it is desirable on the second reading of this bill to state why we in this party regard it as a bill which we should oppose, as we have opposed it, to the end.
W e regard it as ill-conceived, arbitrary, illegal and destructive.
In one respect, Mr. Speaker, I think this bill might be described as almost unique. Often on previous occasions when we have opposed government bills I have felt that I was able, in some measure at any rate, to understand the reasons which moved the government to the passing of the bill, but I confess that here I am in a complete fog. I cannot understand what moves the government to pass this bill. There is an old saying that the heart has its reasons which reason cannot tell, and I can only assume that the government also have reasons which reason cannot tell, and I propose to leave it at
that; but I should like to ask the house to recall very briefly the background which has led us into what seems to me to be a sea of troubles.
The house will remember that this bill is designed to assist in meeting-very inadequately, I think-certain troubles which arose from a most unwise decision of the government in July, 1946, a decision to which they have adhered with what I suggest is unhappy obstinacy. The result of that, as you will recall, Mr. Speaker, was that in a year over a billion dollars of our gold and United States exchange cataracted away. Were there no warnings given the government? Yes, there were warnings given constantly during the session of 1947 and again during the summer after the session had ended. But unfortunately inaction was persisted in constantly until in the middle of November an announcement was made over the air by the Minister of Finance (Mr. Abbott) imposing this tax. This imposition was illegal. In order to try to escape the illegality the minister has had to resort to hair-splitting which, I am sure, was very disagreeable to him. He has had to say that there was no tax, and there was only an indication that parliament would be asked to pass a tax, and that the people need not pay the tax. I am not going to labour the point, Mr. Speaker; I am just going to say it is playing with words-playing with words to say there was no tax when every customs official had been told to act under the notice which had been given; it is playing with words to say there is no tax when people had goods coming from the United States in customs warehouses and could not get them until they paid the tax. As a matter of fact the truth is that it was announced as a tax, intended as a tax, collected from the Canadian people as a tax, and if it was not a tax all I can say is that a great fraud was practised on the Canadian people.
I have just one other remark to make on this question of the lawlessness of this tax, and that is to recall to the memories of hon. gentlemen the fact that when the hon. member for Vancouver-Burrard (Mr. Merritt) asked the Secretary of State for External Affairs (Mr. St. Laurent), an eminent lawyer, whether he considered the tax legal, the hon. member remained glued to his chair.
I have said that the tax, in spite of all the months of delay, was, so far as we could see, passed in a hasty and ill-considered manner. The reason I say that is that it was no sooner passed than it was found necessary to begin to make changes in it. The minister frankly told us the changes were made because they found
Excise Tax Act Amendment

cases of distress. Well, Mr. Speaker, what I want to say to you is that they are going to find more cases of distress and they are going to have to make more changes. Incidentally I understand that in the bill the right is reserved to make still further changes; and while I am on this point I would make the suggestion that this measure will in the end prove to be a ridiculous measure because it will fail in what is intended and I believe the government will be under pressure to make more and more changes.
But I want to make a further point. Notwithstanding the fact that changes have been made to lessen distress-and I am not going into details-there is plenty of distress now. There is plenty of anger and disappointment. There are people whose businesses are being ruined, and they will very properly ask why it is that they were victimized in this way.
If I have given anything approximately fair as a description of the situation which we have at the present time-let me interject here to say what has already been said, that in Bill 3, however much one may object to certain features of it, there were effective powers retained; but in this bill I believe the whole thing is ill-conceived and will not be effective. I now come back to what I was about to say. If I have given anything approximately fair as a description of the confusion, the distress and the difficulty which are being caused by this bill, you will agree with me, Mr. Speaker, and the house will agree, that valid reasons are necessary, strong and overwhelming reasons that the bill is necessary; and I shall look now for a moment at the reasons.
The first reason given, the reason which I think we all thought was the overwhelming one when we got into the debate, was the saving of United States exchange. As to that I wish to make two observations. It is clear that not only was no figure in the minds of the administration when this tax was announced as to what might be saved in that way-there was an estimate with regard to Bill 3, but apparently no estimate here at all, according to the Minister of Finance. Second, though this bill has now been in effect for four months there are still no figures of the slightest value. In answer to the hon. member for Calgary West (Mr. Smith) the minister said the other night-I paraphrase his words-that he had no figures now and doubted if he ever would have any figures which would show him exactly the effect of this bill. At my request he did produce certain figures which he was good enough to give us yesterday, but after examining these

my feeling is that the savings effected are trivial, and it will take a lifetime of the trickle savings of United States exchange which we would make in that way to begin to recover the billion dollars which cataracted away in the early months of 1947.
It is not surprising that a measure of this kind, conceived in iniquity, should have a very dishonourable life-and it certainly has had a dishonourable life so far. It was defeated in committee-
Has it any parents?

And what happened? We then saw really a very shabby spectacle. It was defeated in committee, and I assumed that with the power of its brute majority the government could have found a way within the rules, when it came back to the house, to summon up its-

I thought in doing that, Mr. Speaker, I was following a distinguished precedent, but I bow to your ruling. I shall just say this-

speakerposition: Whip of the Co-operative Commonwealth Federation
speechtext: The Prime Minister did it on February 10.

I shall just say that I regretted, as I think everyone in the house did, that that ruling which we had all heard and which had been made, I venture to say, with the approval of the government, was then overturned by the vote of the government.
I said, Mr. Speaker, that I would be brief, and I have finished. I just want to say that for these reasons and for other reasons which have been given in this house, we believe not only that this bill is a bad bill but that it does not make sense. I am not going to refer to the other reasons. The United States exchange reason was supposed to be the great one. I submit that it is trivial; that there is no evidence that it will have the slightest effect. All the evidence we have is that its effect will be trivial. The other reasons I shall not pause to enumerate, except to say that I think each of them was weaker than the last. They were obviously conjured up in order to support the weakness of the first one. I did not envy the Minister of Finance his task, but it seemed to me as soon as we tried to pin him down to one reason he flitted off to another. I think that was the only thing he could do because each was so weak that he tried to get strength

Excise Tax Act Amendment
from the others, but I think this strength was a very unhappy evidence of weakness and no strength at all.
I now wish to move in amendment, seconded by the hon. member for Calgary West:
That the word "now" be omitted and the words "this day six months" added at the end of the question.

Mr. Speaker, we in this group have carefully considered the provisions of this bill and its general effect, and after due consideration and deliberation we have come to the conclusion that we must oppose the second reading of the measure.
There are several reasons why we feel that this bill is not in the interests of the Canadian people, and these reasons may be summarized as follows:
First, the tax is not necessary for revenue purposes, and it is inflationary.
Second, the tax is an unnecessary burden on the vast majority of the Canadian people.
Third, there is so far no evidence that the tax will have the expected1 result of conserving United States currency by reducing the consumption of United States goods or of domestic goods with United States content, or by creating an over-all current account surplus.
And lastly, in voting for this bill we would condone a serious breach by the government of our constitution.
With respect to the first objection I have mentioned, namely, that the tax is not necessary for revenue purposes, I do not think that it needs further argument, since the minister himself has admitted1 as much. It has not been introduced for that purpose, and especially is it not required for that purpose because of the rumoured budget surplus which is said to be something around $700 million.
The second reason for opposing the bill is that it places an additional unnecessary burden upon the people, and I think that is particularly true of the young people who are just starting out in life. And when we talk about young people, we necessarily have in our minds our veterans who have come back to us and who wish to establish their homes and take their places in this great Canadian family of ours. Their re-establishment is hard enough as it is, with their rent so high, the cost of building materials and other necessities being what it is, and this only makes it harder for them by putting an additional burden upon their shoulders, a burden which I consider absolutely unnecessary.
In view of the representations we have heard from different members from all sides, even the government side, and the evidence to
which we listened while the bill was in resolution stage in committee, very few articles subject to the tax or duty can be considered luxuries. Most of them are necessities, and I think it is altogether wrong to levy an indirect tax upon such articles. It seems to me it is always the common man, the little man with little means, who bears the heavy burden of indirect taxation, and on general principles we in this group are against any increase in indirect taxation.
We must of course consider, and we in this group have considered that there are sections in the bill referring to the repeal of other taxes. We have fully considered this and have come to the conclusion that the new taxes to be imposed are much greater than the relief which will be afforded by the repeal of these taxes as provided in the last few sections of t'he bill.
On page 2131 of Hansard the minister gives figures and indicates that there has been collected close to $6,000,000 in the last three and a half months since the taxes have been imposed. On these figures we must expect that the new tax is imposed by the measure will be considerably greater than the relief which is afforded by the repeal of the tax on sugar and electric current, et cetera.
Our third reason for opposing the bill is that there is no evidence that the measure will have the expected result of conserving United States dollars. The minister explained that there were two principal reasons for the measures: first, reducing the consumption of United States made goods or articles with high United States content, and second, the creating of an over-all current account surplus.
I do not think that the bill will accomplish that purpose, and there was evidence in the committee to that effect. I think I have listened diligently to all the discussion that took place in committee, and to say the least, any evidence that was produced was most unsatisfactory, contradictory and unconvincing.
Take the case of automobiles. The minister quoted figures yesterday that did not seem to me to give any evidence of success in reducing the consumption of United States made goods or goods with high United States content. On the contrary, I rather take the word of the hon. member for Comox-Alberni (Mr. Gibson), who spoke on Monday and who told us that he had been in Windsor and had talked to some manufacturers. He said at page 2483 of Hansard:
I was in Windsor the other day and they assured me that they had enough orders to keep them going for the next two years.

I fail to see how the minister's delight is compatible with his idea of an over-all current account surplus.
On page 2131 of Hansard, on March 11, the minister said, in answer to a question I put to him:
The secondary purpose, if I may so describe it, is to reduce the consumption of articles in this country which for the time being we can do without. I think X explained yesterday afternoon that if we are to continue to export to the war devastated countries of Europe, we must reduce consumption in this country, whether the things we consume are of United States content or not. In other words we must create what I refer to, and what the economists refer to, as an over-all current account surplus.
From that argument I understand the minister to say, and I think I am right, that we must reduce consumption but not that we must reduce production. As a matter of fact he was emphatic, at another time in the committee, that we must reduce consumption and also increase production. I suggest that the figures he quoted with respect to radio sales and the memorandum of the radio manufacturers from which I quoted a moment ago and which appears in yesterday's Hansard, indicate that not only consumption but also production is going down, which I thought the minister was trying to avoid because of his endeavour to create this over-all current account surplus. Taking a bird's-eye view of all we have heard in committee and in explanation of the necessity for this bill, I

fail to see that the minister has established that this taxation measure will conserve American dollars.
Now I come to the fourth objection I quoted, that is the objection in connection with the legal and constitutional aspect. I had intended at the end of my speech to introduce an amendment but will have to refrain from doing so because of the amendment just introduced by the hon. member for Muskoka-Ontario (Mr. Macdonnell). We were going to propose this amendment:
That in the opinion of the house the action of the government in arranging by ministerial announcement for the collection of taxes, of which parliament had not yet been advised and which parliament has not yet 'mposed, is contrary to established parliamentary practice and wdthout constitutional authority.
As I say, I shall not be able to introduce that amendment now, but I should like to say just a few words as to the legal and constitutional aspect.
I spoke on this matter a few weeks ago and shall not repeat what I said then, but I must emphasize again that the action of the government in collecting this tax since last November is entirely illegal and unconstitutional. I will say that the prerogatives of parliament were crucified. I know, of course, that if parliament passes this bill the tax will be made retroactive to November 18 and the crucified body will be resurrected; but, Mr. Speaker, the ugly nail holes will still be there.
The case I quoted in committee a few weeks ago, Bowles v. the Bank of England, only concerned itself with an ordinary budget resolution introduced while the house was in session. This is something altogether different. The minister does not contend that his announcement was a budget resolution. It strikes me that new taxes, yes and even increases in taxes already in existence, are always imposed by way of the budget, at least in British parliaments; and I have been unable to find a case where a measure has been brought in to raise taxes apart from the budget. The budget represents the general financial program of the government for the year. We have always had budgets. They are a development in our constitutional practice. Reading the historic background of the development of the committee of supply and the committee of ways and means, I find that the function of the committee of ways and means is to find the revenue required for the expenditures voted by the committee of supply. In fact in the early period of constitutional government taxes which were to be imposed as recommended by the committee were always earmarked for certain expenditures. Then we had the gradual development of the genera!

budget and the elimination of the special appropriation; but the fundamental principle, the inherent principle is still present even in our modern budget, namely no taxation without need. In other words the people are not to be taxed unless the money is needed for some expenditure for their general benefit or the benefit of the state. This became clear to me on Monday in listening to the citation and quotation of the authorities on the points of order raised at that time, and after I had an opportunity of studying some of those authorities. Therefore I believe the situation which confronts us is unique. In addition to offending against the legal principle laid down in Bowles v. the Bank of England, the action of the government in collecting the tax since November has disregarded the principle that there should be no taxation unless there is need of it.
I would urgently plead with the government that these things should not happen again, and that at this session a bill should be introduced similar to the bill introduced in Great Britain in 1913 so they could act in case of emergency, and also to make budget resolutions legal whenever the budget is introduced. In these times of unrest and fear, Mr. Speaker, particularly fear that the concepts of a foreign ideology are making inroads upon our democratic institutions, we refuse to be parties to a measure which contains that apparent lighthearted and gross disregard of the prerogatives of parliament.

Some of his others have been very good, but I believe this was his best. The natural eloquence which is his I always find very effective, but in listening to him, it did occur to me that he might have used another cross-that is, the cross of gold, upon which William Jennings Bryan refused to see the American people crucified.
All I intend to do today is recite chronologically, I hope, a few facts in connection with this whole matter, and then ask the members of this house if they can find it within their conscience to do what I am going to suggest the government is asking
us to do here. We all know we have a dollar crisis. The fact 'that we knew it months before any action was taken is of no consequence now-I mean in the realities of the situation. The real facts are before us. We all knew there were two wavs of dealing with it. One was by embargoes, by the rationing of the influx of goods, and so on. Tariff item 28 covers coffee, green, imported direct from the country of growth and production, or purchased in bond in the United Kingdom. Unemployment Insurance Act, 1940-
588. Government's contribution to unemployment insurance fund-further amount required, $5,000,000.

Before this item passes I want to say a few words in connection with a situation that has developed since the end of the wrar, when we have had more unemployment than we had during the war years. In most cases the municipal and provincial governments look after unemployables, but neither the municipalities nor provinces nor the dominion government make provision for employable persons who are unemployed. That is the case with persons who have not qualified for unemployment insurance, and those who have exhausted their benefits under that legislation.
In the proposals made by the dominion government to the provinces in 1945 the dominion agreed to take care of that class of unemployed person. Last winter-and perhaps the situation is still not as good-the number of unemployed was larger than at any time since this act came into effect. A great many persons, young men in particular, found themselves unemployed without having sufficient contributions under the act to entitle them to the benefits of the act. I have a letter from which I should like to quote in order to show how people feel about this situation; and while I am on this point I would suggest to the Minister of Labour that perhaps a better public relations job could be done in connection with unemployment insurance than is done. In 1940 when the act was passed there was considerable opposition to it among workers, but I found that when I spoke to them and explained to them the purposes of the act and its limitations, it was accepted as

Supply-Labour
something worth while. I am convinced that much of the criticism of the act is due to a lack of understanding of it and a lack of appreciation of its limitations.
The writer of this letter is a father whose son, seventeen years of age is unemployed. Most hon. members of this house with boys of that age have them at school, but this young fellow was working and had contributed to the unemployment insurance fund for 171 days. He needs 180 days in order to be eligible for benefits. Another young lad referred to in this letter, not a son of the writer, had contributed 178 days. He was two days short of the required number of contributions, and was not eligible when he became unemployed. I am not suggesting that the act should be stretched even for a day to meet cases of this kind.
Might I ask my hon. friend, for my own information, what city that was in?

I have written this man, and I should be very glad to show the minister my letter if he would care to see it. This man feels, and I think rightly so, that something should be done to assist these young fellows when they are not eligible for unemployment insurance. Referring to the boys he says:

I spent five years and eight months in the army, and now I am beginning to wonder what it was all for. I thought we were going to have a better Canada for our sons and daughters, but it looks pretty grim now for our boys and girls. They don't want something for nothing. They want work and a chance to make a living, but at present it looks as if the soup kitchens will have to come back unless those boys and girls can get at least 180' days' work a year.
My suggestion to the minister and the government is that as quickly as possible they revive the proposals made to the provinces in 1945, and call a conference of the provinces in order to have those proposals discussed, and if possible accepted and thus extend protection to young men, and old men as well who cannot qualify for unemployment insurance.
I want the minister to understand that I am not at the moment finding fault with the administration of the act. Those who are charged with its administration must administer it according to its provisions. If they once [DOT]
begin departing from that they will get into trouble, because there will be no line as to where they should stop.

It may be only for a short time, but on the other hand it may be for a considerable time.
During the past few weeks we have heard a good deal about the dangers of communism. I would be the last one to say that it is not dangerous. But we should remember that communism grew out of bad social conditions and the suppression of a people's just aspirations. We are not going to put an end to communism or eliminate it by suppression at this stage. We will eliminate it and prevent its growth only if we can convince the people of this country that their welfare is our consideration at all times. I suggest to the minister that as soon as possible he try to convince his colleagues in the cabinet, if indeed they are not already convinced, that here is a situation that should be remedied, and without delay.

speakerposition: Whip of the Co-operative Commonwealth Federation
speechtext: There were certain questions I planned to ask at this time, but I was glad to hear Mr. Speaker answer some of them at three o'clock this afternoon. My questions had to do with what progress is being made in the matter of salary increases for employees of the House of Commons, and also whether these increases might be made retroactive to the same date that applied in the case of civil servants. I am sure the Speaker noted how pleased the house was with the announcement he made at three o'clock that increases would be forthcoming shortly and that they would be made retroactive to October 1 last. May I ask His Honour the Speaker at this time if he can say whether the matters now under consideration include a pension plan for sessional stenographers, assuming that they meet certain conditions?

I am very glad to take this occasion to call the attention of the house ' to the fact that the Speaker is not only the hon. gentleman who from the Chair has from time to time called the hon. member to order and has to decide whether an amendment is in order or not-
Can we talk back to the hon. gentleman now?

As the hon. member knows, he is at the same time something like the manager of a big office building or a hotel. He is responsible for the restaurant; he is responsible for the cafeteria; he is responsible for giving hon. members efficient and pleasant stenographers and messengers
Supply-Legislation

and good service. I may say that in that respect he is as much interested as anybody- I would say more than anybody-in trying to do everything possible to recognize the good service given by all the employees of the House of Commons. I believe hon. members will give me credit for having tried, since I have been Speaker of the house, to do everything possible to help these people. Last year we considered what we could do to guarantee a position to everybody who is working in this house and to increase their salaries as the salaries of other people working in the government have been increased, to try to be agreeable and to help. Hon. members should not forget-and it is very important- that contrary to the rules in other departments of the administration of the country, the employees of the House of Commons are not responsible to the government nor to the administration of the country; they are responsible to the house. Therefore it is the privilege of the house to employ all the employees that we need for good service in the house, and I believe we should do everything possible to keep that privilege.
I hope that hon. members will understand the explanation that I am giving them. I understand that some hon. members believed from my pronunciation that I am just back from England or that I am living in Toronto, but unfortunately even if my English is not too good I hope that my words will be perfectly understood. The positions of all employees of the house are being considered at the present time by the internal economy commission of the house. A report will be made and tabled in the house. As I said this afternoon in my statement, it is the intention of the government to introduce in the house as soon as possible after Easter a resolution and a bill founded on that resolution in order that those who are entitled to be appointed permanently will be appointed, permanently; salaries will be decided for such and such a job, and I have every reason to believe that all the employees will be perfectly satisfied.

As one who has taken a special interest in all of the employees of the House of Commons, together with my colleague from Ottawa West I must say that I am rising at this time particularly to congratulate our Speaker on the special attention ho has given in the past two years to the staff and to the service in this house. I have confidence that his intentions are good, in the case of employees of this house, and that their fate could not be in better hands. I am sure that justice will be done to any claims which may be made on oehalf of employees of the house.

speakerposition: Whip of the Co-operative Commonwealth Federation
speechtext:
I am sure we are all grateful for the statement that Mr. Speaker has made on this occasion. There are one or two comments I wish to make. His Honour indicated, and I think rightly, that the employees of the House of Commons are in a different category from the employees of the government, and I think it is correct to say that both the members of the House of Commons and the employees themselves want it to remain that way. His Honour referred to this as a privilege, and correctly so. I simply make the obvious remark that privileges carry with them responsibilities and that of course is the reason we are all interested- that is why Mr. Speaker is interested-in meeting our responsibilities to these people.
The Speaker referred to the comparison between employees of the House of Commons and the employees of the government generally. It is true that there have been increases in salaries for many classifications of civil servants, and I hope this will be done for all employees of the House of Commons. I hope that consideration will be given to some of those who have been here a long time and have not had increases for quite a number of years. Some times it happens that an employee's salary in terms of daily wage does not look too bad, but when it is realized that he has been on that same rate per day for a good many years and the cost of living keeps going up, he feels it is unfair to him if he does not get some increase as well.
I was glad to note what the Speaker said, that consideration was being given to all employees. I hoped he would be able to answer my question about stenographers in relation to pension plans. Did his reference to making some members permanent cover that phase of the matter?

I do not wish to make any commitment. After all, I am chairman of the committee which is known as the internal economy commission, and it has to approve a report which will be tabled in the house, but I may say to my hon. friend that I have always been an employer throughout my life, as I am at the present time in this House of Commons, and thank God, I understand the problems of employees, just as I understand, as a father, the problems of my children. I assure him that I will do everything possible, as I have done in the past, to give justice to these people and to give them security. They will receive what they deserve.
I am very sorry that, as the hon. member knows, we were so busy with committees and the business of the house that we could not

settle the matter before Easter. I should very much have liked to make a declaration, for the benefit of the employees of the house, that such a decision has been reached before the Easter recess. to the acoustics of the chamber, now that we have Mr. Speaker himself in the benches. On behalf of the backbenchers, may I say that we would appreciate it if something could be done and done soon, so that all of us in the house, even if we are comparatively new and unimportant, shall feel that we have some part in what is going on.

tion is a responsibility of the Minister of Trade and Commerce, the Minister of Trade and Commerce should pay its bills rather than have it charge a fee to other departments of government for which it performs services. The policy may be right or wrong, but that is the policy.

A serious educational problem confronts the village of Churchill in northern) Manitoba. It has been brought about because of a property situation in Churchill which is peculiar in our Canadian economy. Ninety-nine per cent of the $3,300,000 of property in Churchill is administered by some department of the federal government. The total amount of property taxable for school purposes is only $38,000, and the revenue obtainable from that small amount of taxable property is not sufficient to operate a school at Churchill. It is true there is a public school there now which looks after the needs of thirty-five students, but in addition there are forty students who cannot get into the school and for whom no educational facilities are provided. The situation has been brought to the attention of the department of education of the Manitoba government, which takes the stand that, since there is no taxable property there, they cannot increase the provincial grant to the school at that point. I have talked with the deputy minister of education of Manitoba and he takes the stand that I am giving to the committee. The people in Churchill are anxious that something be done at the earliest possible
moment to provide a suitable school to take care of the educational needs of the pupils at that point, and I submit that they have a very good case for assistance from the federal government. The deputy minister of educa-That is another reason, I submit, why there province the Department of Justice makes an annual grant of $2,550 to the federal district of Stony Mountain for school purposes. I submit therefore that the federal government should recognize the request of the community of Churchill, because most of the property there is federally owned.
The other day a return was brought down, showing the grants made by the federal government for educational purposes, for vocational training, and the grants to the various provinces totalled $225,000 a year. That is another reason, I submit, why there should be federal aid for the public school at Churchill. The community of Churchill is not by any means destitute. The people there are hard working and they are willing and anxious to pay their fair share of educational costs, but because of the peculiar property situation that exists in that community, it is very difficult for them to have a school constructed at that point out of funds raised from local taxation.
There is another point I want to bring out. Five miles out of Churchill there is an army barracks, where quite a number of members of the armed forces live with their wives and families. The federal government immediately recognized the needs of the army and built a school at the barracks to take care of the children. I am not quarreling with that at all. I think the school was necessary, and it was a good thing that the government went ahead and built one, but I say that the people of Churchill are entitled to the same consideration and steps should immediately be taken by some department of the federal government to set aside funds for the construction of a school at Churchill before another term passes. The time for education for young people is limited indeed, and it would be a disgrace if the children living in that area were to lose one more term of school because of inaction either by the federal or the provincial government.

Before this item is carried, may I just pass a few remarks on this deficit of the Canadian National Railways. Those of us who were here in the depression years know perfectly well that from year to year we were faced with very large deficits. It has always seemed to me to be unfair to saddle the railway with at least a great deal of this deficit. Those of us who know the history of the Canadian National Railways realize that the railways which now comprise the Canadian National were taken over at a value which was not warranted at the time and that they are now loaded down with a capitalization upon which they cannot possibly meet all the obligations that they have to meet in various ways. I suggest again to the committee, as I did in the years before the war, and as other hon. members have suggested, that we should reconsider the capitalization of the Canadian National Railways and remove
from that railway a great deal of the deadweight which it carries and which should never have been carried by the railway. If I may put it in this way, it was an error on the part of parliament and the government of Canada, and until we have removed that tremendous burden from the railway it will never be able to make a comparable showing. May I say that it has a depressing effect on the whole of the staff of the railway? They seem to say, Well, we have such an impossible burden; what can we do? If we want efficiency from the employees of the railway we have to give them a chance to be able to show the people of Canada that they are rendering good service and that the railway is not placing an impossible burden on the people of the country. I plead with the government once again to reconsider this whole matter, and when the time comes, to come forward with a recommendation to relieve the railway of a tremendous burden which it should not be called upon to carry.

One thing that the war has proved is that Canada needs a second railway. It is absolutely essential. It is a good, well-managed, serviceable railway, by no means a white elephant, and should be able to earn charges under any proper system of rate making. higher freight rates is rather antiquated if it takes so long? It is over a year since this city was inundated by high-priced lawyers for provinces, railways, the government and others. We should have that streamlined a bit. It should be pointed out also, in answer to the hon. member for Rosetown-Biggar, as my colleague has said, that there has been no increase in rates since the 1930's.
Are you in favour of an increase in rates?

I do not know of anything else in the economy that has not gone up in view of the fact that wages and supplies have increased substantially. I am not in favour of an increase in rates if the railways can maintain adequate service for the people, but I should think the managers of the railways would have to be nothing less than wizards to maintain adequate service with 1948 wages and material costs and 1930 freight rates.
What about calling in six per cent bonds for a change?
What percentage of the capital stock is held in Canada?
The capital stock of the Canadian National is all held in Canada.
None held in Britain?

I do not want to enter into a discussion of freight rates, but what we have to bear in mind is that this country is largely bound together by bands of steel. Our railways are a vital part of confederation and, under ordinary business freight rate conditions, freight rates from many parts of Canada to the coast are prohibitive. It is part of the obligation of maintaining a united Canada to subsidize, if you will, the carrying of freight over long distances in this country. When you think of the distance between Ontario and western Canada, and across the mountains to the coast, and again from Quebec right through to Prince Edward Island, literally thousands of miles of non-revenue producing railway, you realize that a freight rate structure comparable with that of the United States with which we compete is an impossibility in this country. And if we boosted freight rates to do all that the hon. member for Rosedale would ask us to do, I think it would kill the competitive spirit of Canadians in the remote parts of Canada in the marketing of their produce across the seas.

Representations are made to me from time to time -and I fancy they are made to other hon. members-seeking an interpretation respecting the earning power of veterans receiving war veterans allowances, so that they will not be tied down quite so closely in respect of the amount of money they can earn outside their allowances.
Veterans of world war I, particularly, have a strong claim on parliament because of their age, and I think there should not be too much by way of restrictions placed upon the amount they are permitted to earn outside their veterans allowances. I am sure the minister must know of a great many cases of that kind. Now that so many years have gone by, I suggest that we should not be too close in our limitations as they affect these older veterans who, in most instances, have had a pretty difficult time. I hope the leniency the government may have by way of discretion will be afforded these men in a way which would meet the wishes of many veterans throughout the country.

If, as and when the bill in resolution stage on the order paper dealing with veterans allowances should come into force, provision is made therein in connection with war veterans allowances in a manner similar to that having to do with pensions. I cannot comment upon that bill until it is before the house, but I can assure hon. members that the point just made has been borne in mind.

Many representations are made to me in connection with war veterans allowances. I appreciate that the matter is now or shortly will be before the veterans affairs committee and before the house. We can deal with these matters at that time. I would suggest to the minister, however, that any veteran of world war I who is in receipt or who may be in receipt of war veterans allowance should be paid it without any means test whatsoever. The mere fact that he is eligible for war veterans allowance is in itself sufficient proof that he has very little income. Not only should there not be any means test, but for his own welfare he should be encouraged to add as much as possible to his income. It would be good for him, and it will be good for the country.

When the war veterans allowance legislation does come before the house I would strongly urge that consideration be given to imperial veterans who have resided in this country continuously for twenty years. speakerposition: Whip of the Co-operative Commonwealth Federation
speechtext: May I add one sentence? I hope consideration is also being given to including service in England in world war I as service in a theatre of war.

Before this item passes, may I say that up to the present time I believe altogether too much attention has been given to the monetary aspect of our treatment of our returned soldiers. I believe the time has come when the country, the government and the House of Commons as a whole should look upon veterans as assets of Canada, and look upon their case in terms of giving them a living. Up to the present time the whole attitude appears to have been that of giving them an existence. The more meagre and stingy that existence, the better we were satisfied.
This principle is entirely wrong. It must be borne in mind that each of the boys who returned from overseas is a possible father of a Canadian family. We are doing a great deal to increase the population of this country. I can think of no finer blood to go into the future of Canada than the blood of those who went to fight for this country.
I want to see each and every one of those men placed in a position in which, in comfort, he could have and support a family in Canada. If we have that attitude we shall do away with many of the contemptible and disgraceful rules which restrict and hamper and discourage our boys and their wives at every turn. If the general purport of my remarks is taken and applied throughout the whole range of the treatment of veterans in this country, before long we shall find our veterans happy.
At the beginning of the war we used to say that we wanted to ensure to Canadians that no one who went into any of the services would foe any worse off because of his going in, and no one who did not go into the services would be any better off because he did not go.
Many hon. members who were in the house in those days will recall distinctly that such was the purport of the remarks of responsible ministers in the house. We have now gone a long way from the path indicated by that general attitude. I wager that those poor chaps who sat on the floor of the house the other day are far worse off than they would have been if they had not gone. And the worst of it is that, in accordance with the rules being laid down by

the government, I see no means whereby those boys can ever have made up to them the losses they sustained because they went into the services.

speakeroldname: Right Hon. W. L. MACKENZIE KING (Prime Minister):
speakerposition: Prime Minister; President of the Privy Council
speechtext:
That concludes the business. No doubt hon. members will wish to know the proposed order of business immediately after the Easter adjournment. In considering the matter, the government thought it would be advisable to bring forward as soon as possible measures pertaining to the appointment of committees or measures likely to be referred to a special or standing committee. There is a resolution on the order paper in regard to the appointment of a joint committee of both houses of parliament to consider the question of human rights and fundamental freedoms. I assume it would be the wish of hon. members to have that committee appointed forthwith. There is the resolution with respect to the introduction of a bill regarding the Industrial Disputes Investigation Act. It appears as Item No. 9 on today's order paper. That bill of the Minister of Labour is to be referred to a committee. It is therefore advisable it should be introduced at a very early stage after recess. Item No. 20 on today's order paper is a resolution relating to an amendment to the War Veterans Allowance Act to extend the provisions of that act to a neglected child or children, et cetera. The bill founded on that resolution will, I assume, go to the committee on veterans affairs. There is also a resolution in the name of the Secretary of State for the introduction of the measure to amend the Dominion Elections Act to make provision inter alia for an increase in salary of the chief electoral officer. That bill, I assume, will also be referred to a committee.
Business oj the House

There is the measure respecting gold, No. 7 on the order paper today:
Resuming the adjourned debate on the motion of the Minister of Finance for the second reading of Bill No. 7, respecting emergency payments to assist in meeting the increased cost of production of gold.
It was understood, I think, that this measure would be taken up immediately after the measures we have dealt with today. It might be regarded as the first measure to be taken up after the Easter recess. The others I have mentioned might be brought forward in the order most convenient to hon. members.
What I have said will serve as an indication of the measures that may occupy the first few' days of the session after the Easter recess. It is understood that when discussion begins on the estimates, the first to be considered will be those of the Department of External Affairs.

Would the Prime Minister call the committee on printing as soon as we resume on April 5? I understand that committee wants to meet in order to provide for the printing of the evidence of the Hong Kong inquiry.

speakerposition: Prime Minister; President of the Privy Council
speechtext: A day or two after I proposed the motion, the chairman of that committee informed me that he was arranging to have the committee meet at once. He found, however, it would be more convenient to hon. members on the committee if the committee met after the Easter recess. I understand that has been arranged.

Since apparently we have reached the end of today's proceedings, in the absence of the Minister of Mines and Resources (Mr. Glen) I should like to draw the attention of the Prime Minister to the fact that on April 5 the Essex county tourist association is inaugurating Canada's first national wildlife week, which, as the right hon. gentleman knows, was instituted to commemorate the-great work done by the late Jack Miner. They are holding a dinner in Windsor that day and, as the Prime Minister knows, they were very anxious to have him address that meeting. However, since he had made other arrangements and was unable to accept the invitation-
Oh, go on; sit down.

Thanks very much. As the Prime Minister knows, the Minister of National Health and Welfare will be the speaker on that occasion. Since this will be the first time we have had a national wildlife week in Canada, I thought it would be only

fitting for the government to make some announcement that this is going to take place, and that the dinner is being held in Windsor to inaugurate that week.

speakerposition: Prime Minister; President of the Privy Council
speechtext:
It will be a pleasure to have that done. I shall see that something along the lines my hon. friend has mentioned is announced. I am only sorry, as I know the minister of health also is, that my hon. friend himself is not to be the chief speaker at the dinner. He should be, for he was the one who introduced the measure in this house.
Now, Mr. Speaker I suggest that the sitting be suspended until word comes from the other house that the deputy of His Excellency is ready to receive us.

speakerposition: Whip of the Co-operative Commonwealth Federation
speechtext: While we are on the business of the house, I should like to address a question to the Prime Minister. He will recall that some days ago I brought up the matter of the motion of December 8, which still governs the business of the house. I need not go into all the points we raised at that time; I am sure the Prime Minister will remember them quite well. He then indicated that when this point had been reached, that is the Easter recess, and we had dealt with certain measures which were indicated as being of an emergency character, the government would give consideration to bringing in some other motion to govern the business of the house from now on, and at least make more convenient our procedure from day to day.

speakerposition: Prime Minister; President of the Privy Council
speechtext: Yes. It is the intention of the government to do exactly as I said and have a motion brought in on one of the opening days after the recess.

With respect to the business of the house, I want to ask the Prime Minister when the committee in regard to rules is going to operate. After the farce we have seen here in the past week, I think it is time that committee met, and it should be the first business of this house to see that it does meet.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext: I suggest that it bring in a rule against repetitious debates in committee, too.
I did not say that, but why not have it done?

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext:
My hon. friend's party
have been the worst offenders.

I do not know anyone who needs it more than the minister does.

The Royal Assent

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext: I have not been repetitious.

speakerposition: Prime Minister; President of the Privy Council
speechtext: As my hon. friend will recall, I brought on the motion for the establishment of that committee some weeks ago. It has been left to the members of the committee themselves to decide when they should meet. His Honour the Speaker stated, I believe, that a meeting would take place during the recess or immediately after.

I assume that the committee has a chairman. The matter was raised by the hon. member for Peel within the last week, and we now see the absolute necessity of doing something to avoid all the nonsense we have been through during the past ten days.

I can assure the hon. member for Calgary West, as I assured the hon. member for Peel, that I am anxious to have the committee meet, and it is my intention to call a meeting right after the Easter recess. I have just received information that it will be about half an hour before we are invited to proceed to the other chamber, so I would suggest that this sitting be suspended.
At 9.10 p.m. the sitting was suspended.
At 9.20 p.m. the sitting was resumed.
